title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite, release notes, known issues, and runbooks
author: Priya Nair
summary: Comprehensive reference for the serving runtime: architecture overview, kernel scheduling design, profiling/playbook steps, benchmarking harness and metrics, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks.
content:
Overview

This page consolidates core documentation for Redwood Inference's serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling strategy, profiling/playbooks, benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, and operational runbooks. It is intended for engineers on the serving-runtime, infra, and SRE teams and for any on-call responders.

Contents
1. Architecture overview
2. Kernel scheduling design
3. Profiling playbook (how-to)
4. Benchmarking suite and test matrix
5. Release notes (selected items)
6. Known issues and mitigations
7. Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)
8. Team wiki and related resources

1) Architecture overview

Purpose: The serving runtime implements a low-latency, high-throughput inference engine that supports multi-tenant hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. This section summarizes components, data flow, and SLOs.

High-level components (logical):
- API Router: validates requests, enforces quotas, routes to tenants/slots.
- Router/Policy layer: smart routing decisions (latency-first, cost-first, region-preference, fallback model variants).
- Request Dispatcher: maintains request queues, admission control, and per-model batching policies.
- Batching Engine: continuous batching service that assembles micro-batches for the GPU execution pipeline while honoring latency SLOs and priority policies.
- Executor: the GPU inference process that runs compiled kernels, manages KV cache, and handles streaming outputs.
- KV cache service: prefix cache for chat-like workloads; supports cache warming and invalidation protocols.
- Metrics & Tracing: detailed telemetry (per-token latency, GPU occupancy, kernel execution time, NVTX traces).
- Control Plane: deployment, model versioning, rollout and fallback policies.

SLOs and operational targets
- Small-model (<=7B) interactive SLO: p95 latency <= 120 ms for 256-token requests, p99 <= 300 ms.
- Medium-model (7B-30B) interactive SLO: p95 <= 250 ms for 512-token requests, p99 <= 600 ms.
- Throughput baseline: target sustained tokens/sec per GPU depends on model/quantization (documented in benchmarking section).
- Error budget policy: 99.9% availability monthly for hosted endpoints; dedicated contracts may have stricter SLA.

Ownership and escalation
- Primary owners: serving-runtime team (pager: #serving-runtime on Slack).
- Secondary owners: eng-sre (for infra/network), eng-infra (for cluster-level issues).

2) Kernel scheduling design

Goals: maximize GPU utilization and token throughput while meeting per-request latency SLOs and avoiding noisy-neighbor interference.

Key concepts and techniques:
- Priority queues: requests are categorized into latency-sensitive (interactive) and throughput-sensitive (batch) queues. Interactive queues get admission weight and preemption capability.
- Preemptible execution: long-running throughput jobs are scheduled on lower-priority CUDA streams and may yield to interactive streams when latency thresholds approach SLO.
- Stream assignment: each logical request maps to a CUDA stream for overlapping host-to-device transfers and kernel execution. We limit concurrent streams per GPU to reduce context switching.
- Kernel fusion & selection: the compilation pipeline chooses fused kernels (attention + feed-forward fused ops) when latency benefit > 5% and memory overhead within budget. We prefer fused kernels for interactive workloads.
- Dynamic kernel selection: at runtime we select kernel implementations based on sequence length, batch size, and quantization format (FP16, FP8, INT8). Kernel profile table is maintained in the model catalog.
- Cooperative scheduling with KV cache: cache-hit requests can avoid KV recomputation; scheduling accounts for cache locality and warms hot prefixes onto local GPU memory to reduce host<->device transfers.

Scheduling parameters and thresholds (operational knobs)
- interactive_max_wait_ms: 8 ms (max time a request may wait to form a small batch).
- max_streams_per_gpu: 32 (soft limit; tuned per hardware family).
- preempt_threshold_pct: 80% (when GPU utilization crosses this, throughput jobs are throttled).
- kernel_switch_latency_budget_ms: 1.5 ms (allowed overhead for switching to a faster fused kernel).

3) Profiling playbook (how-to)

When to profile:
- Regressions in p95/p99 latency after a deploy.
- Unusual drop in tokens/sec or sudden increase in GPU memory usage.
- High variance in latency across identical requests.

Quick triage steps (high level):
1. Confirm scope: identify affected routes/models/tenants and timeframe using dashboards.
2. Capture telemetry: preserve relevant traces (distributed traces, sampled nvtx traces, dense metrics around the incident window).
3. Reproduce: run the failing workload in a staging environment with identical model config and input distribution.
4. Profile: collect GPU and CPU profiles as below.
5. Analyze hotspots and determine mitigation (kernel change, scheduling tweak, config rollback, CPU bottleneck, or infra issue).
6. Postmortem and action items.

Profiling tools and commands
- Lightweight (prod-safe): enable NVTX ranges around request lifecycle and collect lightweight perf counters via Prometheus exporters (kernel time, memory allocs, occupancy).
- Deep GPU profiling (staging only): Nsight Systems export (nsys) and Nsight Compute (ncu) for kernel-level latencies. Example commands (staging):
  - Capture system-wide timeline: nsys profile -o /tmp/nsys_trace --trace=cuda,osrt --capture-range=launch --sample=none -- python3 bench/run_inference_staging.py --model llama-2-13b --seq 1024 --concurrency 4
  - Kernel microprofile: ncu --set full --target-processes all --export /tmp/ncu_report -- python3 bench/run_inference_staging.py --model ...
- CPU profiling: perf, py-spy, or Google gperftools depending on the service language. Use flamegraphs to identify GC or scheduling stalls.

What to capture in a profiling run
- Request-level: request id, arrival timestamp, queue wait time, batch size, sequence length, whether KV cache hit, model version.
- Kernel-level: per-kernel latency, bytes transferred H2D/D2H, GPU occupancy, SM utilization, memory bandwidth.
- System-level: GPU memory usage, temperature, process-level CPU usage, NIC stats.

Interpreting results (common patterns)
- High host-to-device transfer time: check for large input tensors, PCIe bandwidth saturation, or cache misses. Mitigation: enable pinned memory transfers, reduce host copies, decrease batch buildup.
- Low occupancy but high kernel latency: kernel implementation may be sub-optimal for this sequence length. Mitigation: switch to alternative kernel implementation or fallback to non-fused kernel.
- Spikes in CPU time before launching kernels: serialization or Python GIL/GC pauses. Mitigation: offload serialization to C++ shim or increase worker threads.

4) Benchmarking suite and test matrix

Purpose: provide reproducible throughput/latency measurements across model variants, quantization profiles, hardware families, and realistic request mixes.

Test harness components:
- bench/run_bench.py: orchestrates load generation, telemetry capture, and result aggregation.
- configs/: YAML configs that describe model, sequence lengths, concurrency, request distributions, and client-side batching.
- collectors/: scripts that aggregate Prometheus, NVTX, and GPU metrics into a single CSV/JSON for postprocessing.

Canonical workloads (examples)
- Chat short-turns: 30% requests with seq_in 32, seq_out 64; 70% cache warmups.
- Document summarization: single request seq_in 2048, seq_out 512.
- Mixed PLG tracer: mixes incremental streaming requests to emulate product traffic.

Sample benchmark command
- python3 bench/run_bench.py --config configs/llama-2-13b/fp16/interactive-512.yaml --duration 600 --collector nsys --results /tmp/bench_llama13b_interactive.json

Key metrics to record
- p50/p95/p99 latency (ms) per request type and sequence length.
- tokens/sec (sustained) per GPU and per-cluster.
- GPU metrics: average SM occupancy, achieved occupancy, memory utilization, compute utilization.
- Cost proxy: tokens/sec per $/hour for target cloud SKU.

Benchmarking result table (example rows as CSV in results):
- model,quant,hardware,seq,batch,concurrency,p50_ms,p95_ms,p99_ms,tokens_per_sec,gpu_occupancy_pct,gpu_mem_gb
- llama-2-13b,fp16,A100-80GB,512,4,8,45,120,220,1200,78,32

Calibration and acceptance criteria
- New kernel/profile changes must not increase p95 by > 8% on the canonical interactive workload.
- Quantization candidates must be validated for quality (embedding/accuracy checks) and show >1.8x tokens/sec improvement vs FP16 for acceptance.

5) Release notes (selected items since 2026-10)

2027-03-01 (v2.9.0-runtime)
- Added dynamic kernel selection for fused-attention implementations; improves p95 for medium-length sequences by ~12% on A100.
- Introduced interactive_max_wait_ms config to reduce tail latency regressions.
- Bench harness: added cost proxy metric and automated reporter for regression gating.

2026-12-15 (v2.8.4-runtime)
- Fix: reduced host-to-device copy overhead for chat workloads by implementing pinned memory buffers.
- Known issue: enabling pinned buffers on some older GPU driver versions may increase memory pressure; see known issues section.

6) Known issues and mitigations

ISSUE: driver 510.x regression causing intermittent kernel launch timeouts on T4 fleet.
- Symptom: sporadic 10-30s stalls followed by recovery.
- Mitigation: pin fleet to driver 470.x or apply vendor patch. On affected hosts, enable fallback to CPU for short windows (configurable via preemptible_throttle).

ISSUE: pinned memory increases mem pressure on constrained hosts when many concurrent small requests are active.
- Symptom: OOM on GPU or host memory swap.
- Mitigation: set pinned_buffer_pool_size_mb to a conservative value (default 512 MB) for small-host instances and enable adaptive pooling.

ISSUE: fused kernel produces numerical mismatch for extreme sequence lengths on INT8 quantized models.
- Symptom: stray token probability shifts causing quality regressions in rare prompts.
- Mitigation: fallback to FP16 kernel for sequences > 4096 or when quantization-quality checks fail. Add automated regression tests in the bench harness.

7) Runtime runbooks (incident procedures)

Runbook: High request p95/p99 latency (interactive)
1. Check dashboards: identify affected routes, models, and hosts (time window, error spikes, and whether it's global or single AZ).
2. Isolate scope: use trace sampling to determine if queue wait times or kernel execution times are driving the tail.
3. If queue wait time high: temporarily increase worker threads or reduce interactive_max_wait_ms to allow smaller batches to flow.
4. If kernel time high: enable emergency kernel fallback (toggle to alternative kernel implementation) or scale up dedicated capacity (add more replicas with hot-warm split).
5. If GPU memory pressure: drain low-priority throughput jobs from the affected hosts and evict large cached prefixes.
6. Post-incident: capture full nvtx and nsys traces for root-cause analysis and file a regression ticket if deploy-related.

Runbook: OOM on GPU during model load or runtime
1. Evict model variants if using multi-model GPU hosts and restart the failing executor.
2. If host-level memory fragmentation suspected, reboot the host or restart the GPU driver after scheduled maintenance window.
3. Apply model-quantization fallback or reduce per-model max_cache_size_mb.
4. Notify eng-infra if repeated across hosts (suspect driver or kernel leak).

Runbook: Sudden drop in tokens/sec cluster-wide
1. Check infra layers: GCE/AWS scheduler, NIC errors, cloud autoscaler events.
2. Check GPU telemetry for thermal throttling or power capping.
3. Confirm no recent rollout: roll back runtime if a recent deploy correlates with the drop.

Appendix A - Example config snippets

# example scheduling config (YAML)
# interactive_max_wait_ms: maximum time to assemble a small latency-sensitive micro-batch
interactive_max_wait_ms: 8
max_streams_per_gpu: 32
preempt_threshold_pct: 80
kernel_switch_latency_budget_ms: 1.5

Appendix B - Bench guardrails and PR checklist
- All PRs that change kernel selection, batching logic, or scheduling parameters must include:
  1) Bench results for canonical interactive workload (p50/p95/p99).
  2) Resource usage (GPU occupancy, mem usage).
  3) Quality regression checks for quantized models (embedding/LLM evals).
  4) Rollout plan (canary % and rollback criteria).

Maintenance and updates
- This page is maintained by the serving-runtime docs owner (Priya Nair). Major updates should be coordinated with reviewers listed above.
- For feature work (kernel/fusion/quant changes), link the change to a bench run id and the related ADR in /confluence/architecture-and-standards/decision-records.
